title: Running Containers with Options ⚙️
description: Go beyond the basics: run containers in the background, name them, and map ports.

slides.title: Recap: `docker run` 🔁
slides.content:
# The Most Important Command

```bash
docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE [COMMAND] [ARG...]
```

So far we used it without options:
```bash
docker run hello-world
```

Now we'll supercharge it with flags that make containers useful in real projects.

slides.title: Run in the Background: `-d` 🤫
slides.content:
# Detached Mode

By default, `docker run` attaches your terminal to the container. If the container runs a long‑lived process (like a web server), your terminal stays occupied.

With `-d` (detached), the container runs in the background and prints the container ID.

```bash
docker run -d nginx
```

This starts an Nginx web server and returns immediately.

Check it with `docker ps` – you’ll see the container running.

quizData.question: What does the `-d` flag do in `docker run -d nginx`?

options.text: It deletes the container after it stops.
It runs the container in detached (background) mode.
It downloads the image if not present.

quizData.explanation: `-d` stands for 'detach'. It tells Docker to run the container in the background and print the container ID.

slides.title: Name Your Containers: `--name` 🏷️
slides.content:
# Friendly Names

Docker auto‑generates random names like `brave_curie` or `jovial_kowalevski`. For real work, you want predictable names.

```bash
docker run -d --name my-web nginx
```

Now you can refer to the container by `my-web` instead of its long container ID.

**Note:** Container names must be unique. You cannot have two containers with the same name.

quizData.question: You can reuse the same container name after deleting the old container.
quizData.explanation: Names must be unique among all containers (running or stopped). Once you delete a container, the name becomes available again.

slides.title: Port Mapping: `-p` 🌉
slides.content:
# Exposing Container Services

Containers have their own network. By default, their services are not reachable from your host.

Use `-p host_port:container_port` to create a bridge.

```bash
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx
```

- `80` is the port **inside** the container (Nginx default).
- `8080` is the port on your **host**. Open `http://localhost:8080` in your browser.

You can also map to random host port using `-P` (with EXPOSE in image).

quizData.question: If you run `docker run -d -p 3000:80 nginx`, which port should you access in your browser?
quizData.explanation: The syntax is `host:container`. So `3000` is the host port, and `80` is the container port. Access `http://localhost:3000`.

slides.title: Other Handy `run` Options 🔧
slides.content:
# More Useful Flags

- `--rm` – automatically remove the container when it exits. Great for one‑off tasks.
- `-e` – set environment variables inside the container (`-e MY_VAR=value`).
- `--restart` – set restart policy (`no`, `on-failure`, `always`, `unless-stopped`).
- `-v` – mount a volume (we’ll cover volumes later).

**Example – a self‑cleaning temporary container:**
```bash
docker run --rm ubuntu echo "I will be deleted after I finish"
```

quizData.question: Which flag makes Docker automatically delete the container when it stops?
quizData.explanation: `--rm` is perfect for temporary containers. After the main process exits, the container is automatically removed, keeping your system tidy.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Keep it clean with `--rm`
When experimenting, always add `--rm` so you don’t end up with dozens of stopped containers. Combine with `docker ps -a` to verify.
